Re:   New York Independent System Operator, Inc., Proposed Tariff Revisions to 
Establish New Large Load Integration Procedures and Related Market 
Participation Provisions, Request to Hold Show Cause Proceedings in Continued 
Abeyance, and Request for One-Week Extension of the Comment Period, Docket 
No. ER27-___-000  
Dear Secretary Reese, 
In accordance with Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)1 and Part 35 of the 
Commission’s regulations,2 the New York Independent System Operator, Inc. (“NYISO”) 
submits proposed revisions to its Open-Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) and Market 
Administration and Control Area Services Tariff (“Services Tariff”).3  The proposed revisions 
establish new Large Load Integration Procedures (“LLIP”) and related market participation 
provisions.  They are intended to fully satisfy the concerns raised by the Commission in its 
Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act (“Show Cause 
Order”)4 to the extent that they involve issues that are within the scope of the NYISO’s tariff 
filing authority.5   
The proposals in this filing are designed to account for issues and conditions in the 
NYISO region.  They build on the NYISO’s recently adopted Standard Interconnection 
Procedures and on various NYISO-specific independent entity variations that are foundational to 
the interconnection process in New York and that bring many benefits.  They also: (i) address the 
unprecedented near-term resource adequacy challenges, driven in large part by an expected 
influx of large loads, that the NYISO now faces; (ii) leverage the NYISO’s existing “financial” 
transmission reservation service model to maximize the benefits to flexible large loads and other 
customers; and (iii) contain various mechanisms to protect customers.    
 
The NYISO’s proposals recognize that NYISO is a single-state entity whose operational 
boundaries coincide with the retail rate and resource adequacy jurisdiction of the New York State

Public Service Commission (“NYPSC”).  The NYPSC has separately launched a proceeding to 
address state-jurisdictional interconnection reforms that are likely to influence the evolution of 
Commission-jurisdictional large load rules in New York.6   
 
 
The NYISO’s proposal incorporates a compromise approach to resource adequacy 
requirements, the State Exempt Load Project exception, that is intended to reconcile the 
NYISO’s reliability responsibilities with the NYPSC’s resource adequacy authority in a manner 
that is consistent with cooperative federalism principles.7  More generally, the NYISO has 
carefully considered and sought to adhere to the Commission’s guidance on large load 
jurisdictional issues and to respect both federal and state authority while still producing a 
proposal that effectively meets the NYISO region’s needs. 
 
Parts II and III of this transmittal letter describe the NYISO’s proposed new LLIP and 
explain its benefits.  Among other things, Parts II and III: (i) describe the NYISO’s proposed 
definition of “Large Load,” which reflects minor changes to the Show Cause Order’s noted 
version to reflect NYISO’s circumstances; (ii) incorporate clear and detailed large load 
interconnection rules into the NYISO OATT; (iii) introduce transition rules that balance the 
timely implementation of the new procedures while avoiding disruptions to existing commercial 
arrangements that have achieved reasonable progress; (iv) promote timely Large Load 
interconnections; (v) provide for new types of Commission-jurisdictional transmission services, 
i.e, “Firm Withdrawal Service” and “Non-Firm Withdrawal Service”, that reflect the unique 
characteristics of both the NYISO’s transmission model and of co-located Large Loads, Large 
Load with behind the meter generation, and flexible Large Loads that are able to limit their use 
of the system; (vi) delineate the division of responsibilities between the NYISO and 
transmission-owning utilities under the LLIP; (vii) include detailed application and readiness 
requirements to deter speculative projects that could unduly shift costs onto existing customers; 
(viii) establish a Large Load Integration Study Process; (ix) address the identification and cost 
allocation of upgrades; and (x) describe how alternative transmission technologies will be 
considered.   
Part IV of this transmittal letter describes the various new market participation provisions 
that the NYISO is proposing to account for the proliferation of Large Loads and to support its 
Large Load reforms.  These proposals include revised and new market rules to govern: (i) Large 
Loads eligible to be served via Firm Withdrawal Service, (ii) Large Loads or portions thereof 
and an “Associated Resource(s)” that enter into a “Co-Located Arrangement” or “Partner 
Resource Arrangement” so that the Large Load may be served via some amount of Firm 
Withdrawal Service; (iii) Large Loads or portions thereof served via Non-Firm Withdrawal 
Service and/or are designated Zero Withdrawal Service Loads; (iv) the co-location of Large 
Loads with Supply.

Within this framework, the NYISO would, among other things: (i) establish a rule under 
which Non-Firm Withdrawal Service would be curtailed when the applicable nodal Locational-
Based Marginal Price (“LBMP”) for a Large Load reaches $200 MW/h; (ii) explain how 
different categories of Large Loads will interact with the NYISO’s capacity market Demand Side 
Resource rules; (iii) subject all Large Loads to fees and charges on a gross load basis; (iv) adopt 
a System Reliability Benefit Fee applicable to Large Loads served by some amount of Non-Firm 
Withdrawal Service to allocate costs to them that are roughly commensurate with the benefits 
they receive from ICAP Resources and the value of the reliability services that they provide; (v) 
apply certain data reporting requirements to all Large Loads; (vi) introduce a new Co-Located 
and Limited Load Configuration market participation model; (vii) use Associated Resource rules 
tied to NYISO Capacity Regions in lieu of the Show Cause Order’s “electrically proximate 
resource;” (viii) address the extent to which Demand Side Resources and Aggregations may 
become Associated Resources; (ix) enhance the NYISO’s DER and Aggregation participation 
model rules; (x) sunset the NYISO’s existing BTM:NG Resource program; and (xi) update the 
existing “buyer-side” capacity market power mitigation measures to reflect new issues presented 
by Large Loads and emerging resource adequacy challenges in New York.    
Part V explains why the NYISO is not proposing to adopt the three new transmission 
services that the Commission established in the PJM Co-Location Order8 and provides additional 
information regarding the benefits of the NYISO’s established financial transmission reservation 
model and new Withdrawal Services.    
New York’s Commission-jurisdictional transmission-owning utilities are concurrently 
making separate FPA Section 205 filings to address Show Cause Order matters that fall under 
their reserved filing rights.  As discussed in Part VI of this transmittal letter, the traditional New 
York Transmission Owners (“NYTOs”)9 are making a contemporaneous FPA Section 205 filing 
that will propose various tariff revisions to the NYISO OATT, principally to Rate Schedule 5, 
and add several new pro forma agreements to the NYISO OATT.  Among other things the 
NYTOs will submit a new two-party pro forma cost recovery agreement to address the cost-
shifting issues discussed in the Show Cause Order.  The non-incumbent transmission owners 
(“NTOs”)10 that were subject to the Show Cause Order will be making concurrent Section 205 
filings to address matters that implicate their reserved filing rights and that reflect the structural 
differences between them and the NYTOs.  The NYISO believes that its Section 205 filing, in 
combination with the NYTO’s and NTOs’, will address all of the issues raised by the Show 
Cause Order.11

Part VII explains that the Commission should determine that this filing is just, 
reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory and issue an order accepting it under the FPA Section 
205 standard of review without requiring any modifications or additional procedures.  At the 
same time, the NYISO consents to the Commission’s exercise of its authority to modify or sever 
any element of the NYISO’s proposed tariff revisions to the maximum extent permitted by law.   
As noted below in Part VIII, the NYISO’s proposal has evolved substantially in response 
to extensive stakeholder feedback.  The NYISO’s proposed tariff revisions received the super-
majority stakeholder approval required under the NYISO’s shared governance model to 
authorize its submission under FPA Section 205.    
Part IX below explains that the NYISO is requesting a February 1, 2027 effective date for 
the LLIP-related tariff provisions described in Parts II and III, June 1, 2028 for the Large Load 
market participation provisions set forth in Part IV, and May 1, 2029 for the sunsetting of the 
existing BTM:NG Resource program which is described in Part IV.I.       
Consistent with the  August 14, 2026 letter order (“Abeyance Order”)12 in the Show 
Cause Order proceeding, the NYISO respectfully requests in Part X below that the Commission 
hold the Section 206 proceedings initiated by the Show Cause Order in continued abeyance 
pending action on this filing.  If the Commission accepts this filing it should also issue an order 
terminating the Show Cause Order proceeding with respect to the NYISO.13   
Finally, the NYISO asks that the Commission briefly extend the comment period on this 
filing from the standard twenty-one days to twenty-eight days. As noted in Part XI a modest 
extension would provide interested parties with additional time to address the numerous, 
complex, and consequential issues implicated by the NYISO’s proposals and by the Show Cause 
Order.  A one-week extension would also accommodate the Thanksgiving holiday and should 
not hinder the Commission’s review because the NYISO’s earliest requested effective date is 
more than two weeks after the end of the standard sixty-day notice period.

II. 
THE NYISO’S PROPOSED TARIFF REVISIONS TO ESTABLISH AND 
IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD INTEGRATION PROCEDURES 
A. 
Large Load 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission found that it would be reasonable to define a 
large load as “a new commercial or industrial customer, located at a single site behind one or 
more points of interconnection, and that has a peak load of 50 MW or greater and interconnects 
to the transmission system at a voltage level of greater than 69 kV, and is not part of a co-
location arrangement.”14  The Commission stated that an “appropriate definition, including a 
load size and interconnection voltage threshold, should be based on the characteristics of 
NYISO’s transmission system.”15 
The NYISO proposes to adopt the Commission’s definition of Large Load with certain 
variations described below.  In particular, the NYISO proposes to define Large Load for its 
OATT and Services Tariff as follows: 
Large Load shall mean a commercial or industrial Load located at a single site or 
in close proximity, behind one or more Points of Interconnection, that has a peak 
Load of 50 MW or greater connected to the New York State Transmission 
System, which is subject to and has completed the applicable requirements of the 
Large Load Integration Procedures in Attachment LL of the ISO OATT.  For 
purposes of this definition, Load shall be considered to be located “in close 
proximity” if it: (i) is located within 2 miles and 2 electrical buses and (ii) is 
electrically located in the same Capacity Region.16 
First, the NYISO proposes to provide that the Load may be located either at a single site 
or in close proximity.  As indicated in the definition, the NYISO proposes to define “in close 
proximity” to mean that the Load is both: (i) located within 2 miles and 2 electrical buses and (ii) 
is electrically located in the same Capacity Region.  Load projects could be spread across a 
geographic area that necessitate more than one Point of Interconnection (e.g., data center 
campus) and should be addressed as a single project in assessing their system impacts.  The 
requirement for both 2 miles and 2 buses constitutes a reasonable basis for defining close 
proximity based on the different topography across the New York State Transmission System, 
as: (i) there are parts of the system in which 2 buses are located many miles away from each 
other (e.g. upstate New York), and (ii) additionally, there are parts of the system in which 
numerous buses can be located within 2 miles (e.g. New York City).  In addition, it is necessary 
that a single Large Load be located within a single Capacity Region for purposes of the

Second, the NYISO proposes not to exclude load that is part of a co-location arrangement

Finally, for purposes of the transition requirements for load projects currently

clarify that the requirements applicable to Large Loads in its tariffs apply to those load projects 
that were subject to and completed the requirements in the Large Load Integration Procedures.   
B. 
Proposed New Transmission Services for Large Loads 
The NYISO’s proposed rules for the participation of Large Loads in the ISO 
Administered Markets vary depending on a Large Load’s Withdrawal Service(s)17 
classification(s) as determined in the LLIP.18  Depending on the results of the LLIP, a Large 
Load may be eligible to receive Firm Withdrawal Service19 and/or Non-Firm Withdrawal 
Service20 and/or to be a Zero Withdrawal Service Load.21  
The new Firm and Non-Firm Withdrawal Services are described in new Section 3A of the 
NYISO OATT.  They are new forms of Commission-jurisdictional Transmission Service with 
terms and conditions that reflect the unique operational and reliability challenges that providing 
transmission service to Large Loads presents to the NYISO system.  These challenges are 
described in the Altman Affidavit.  In addition, as described in Part V below and in the Harvey 
Affidavit the design of new Firm and Non-Firm Withdrawal Services is consistent with the 
NYISO’s existing financial reservation transmission service model.  The creation of the new 
Withdrawal Services is responsive to the Show Cause Order’s preliminary finding that the 
NYISO’s tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it does not include transmission 
services for Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Eligible Load, or on

For convenience, this transmittal letter sometimes refers informally to the NYISO 
providing Firm or Non-Firm Withdrawal Service “to” Large Loads or to Large Loads “taking” or 
“receiving” them.  Such references are meant to encompass instances where a Transmission 
Customer is taking the services on a Large Load’s behalf in which a Large Load is acting as its 
own Load-Serving Entity.  They should not be construed as indicating that Firm or Non-Firm 
Withdrawal Services are not Commission-jurisdictional forms of transmission service.     
Firm Withdrawal Service would be available to Large Loads that are determined, through 
the LLIP, not to cause adverse impacts or violations to resource adequacy or transmission 
security or which adverse impacts or violations are mitigated as described in Part II.G.i.23   
A Large Load, or any portion thereof, taking Firm Withdrawal Service will be able to use 
the transmission system to serve its load in a price-agnostic manner and will be treated in the 
same manner as other customers taking firm Transmission Service, including with respect to 
curtailment priority.  Firm Withdrawal Service will be subject to NYISO emergency operating 
procedures, and Large Loads taking such service may be required to curtail for reliability needs 
consistent with the priority treatment that load resources receive today.24  All requests for Firm 
Withdrawal Service will have the same reservation priority, and Firm Withdrawal Service will 
have the same priority as Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service.  Firm Withdrawal Service 
will have priority over Non-Firm Withdrawal Service.25 
Non-Firm Withdrawal Service would be made available to dispatchable Large Loads that 
are deemed to cause violations or adverse impacts to resource adequacy and/or transmission 
security, which violations or adverse impacts are not mitigated as described in Part II.G.i.26  
Large Loads taking Non-Firm Withdrawal Service will be eligible to withdraw Energy from the 
transmission system, subject to a bid cap and other necessary requirements.27  As described in 
Part IV.B.ii.b, the NYISO proposes to use a mandatory bid cap of $200/MWh as the mechanism 
to curtail Non-Firm Large Loads to avoid adverse impacts to the system.  Non-Firm Withdrawal 
Service will be subject to NYISO dispatch and emergency operating procedures.28  
Zero Withdrawal Service Loads will be either (a) a Limited Withdrawal Service Load in 
a Co-Located and Limited Load Configuration (“CLLC”), or (b) a Co-Located Located Load in a 
Co-Located Local Generator Configuration (“CLGC”).  Zero Withdrawal Service Loads will be 
Large Loads that have not requested Withdrawal Service rights and will not be authorized to 
withdraw Energy from the NYS Transmission System.  As described in Part IV.B.ii.e, a Zero

C. 
Large Load Integration Procedures 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission found that, notwithstanding the NYISO’s 
existing load interconnection requirements, the NYISO’s existing OATT appears to be unjust 
and unreasonable because it does not include provisions that address with sufficient clarity and 
consistency the study process for the provision of transmission service to Eligible Customers on 
behalf of large loads, including the unique operational characteristics of large loads.29   
The NYISO proposes to establish new Large Load Integration Procedures, which will be 
located in Attachment LL to the OATT.30  The procedures include clear and detailed 
requirements pursuant to which: (i) an Eligible Customer may submit a Large Load Integration 
Request for the evaluation of the proposed interconnection of a Large Load Project to the New 
York State Transmission System and (ii) the NYISO and Transmission Owners, as applicable, 
will evaluate the proposed interconnection, identify any Attachment Facilities and Network 
Upgrades required for the reliable interconnection of such project and their estimated costs and 
schedule, and determine the project’s Firm Withdrawal Service or Non-Firm Withdrawal Service 
amounts or, if requested, its eligibility to proceed as a Zero Withdrawal Service Load. 
The NYISO highlights in Part II.C.i key elements of its proposed Large Load Integration 
Procedures.  The NYISO then provides a high-level overview of the new procedures in Part 
II.C.ii and in the figure in Attachment VI.  Finally, the NYISO describes the new procedures in 
detail in Parts II.D through III, including demonstrating that the procedures are just and 
reasonable and address the findings of the Show Cause Order in light of the NYISO’s distinct 
planning framework and market structure, its role as a single-state independent system operator 
(“ISO”), and other New York-specific conditions.  The proposed procedures are supported by the 
affidavit of Thinh T. Nguyen, NYISO Senior Manager of Interconnection Projects (“Nguyen 
Affidavit”). 
i. 
Key Elements of the Large Load Integration Procedures 
a) 
Clear and Detailed Procedures  
The NYISO proposes in this filing to establish new Large Load Integration Procedures as 
described in detail in Parts II.D through III that set forth clear and detailed tariff requirements 
concerning the application for and the study of the proposed interconnection of Large Load 
Projects.  The NYISO proposes that these new procedures replace its existing load 
interconnection requirements set forth in Sections 3.9 and 4.5 of the OATT, subject to certain 
transition requirements.  
b) 
Effective Date and Transition Process

The NYISO proposes that the Large Load Integration Procedures have an effective date 
of February 1, 2027, as described in Parts II.D.ii and IX.  The NYISO also proposes to establish 
transition rules that balance timely implementing the new requirements adopted in response to 
Show Cause Order with minimizing disruptions to those projects that have already completed or 
progressed to certain defined milestones in the NYISO’s existing load interconnection process.  
As described in Part II.D.ii, the NYISO proposes to establish two transition groups – Transition 
Group A and Transition Group B – for projects that meet the definition of Large Load and satisfy 
certain tariff-prescribed milestones and requirements.  Projects in Transition Group A must have 
advanced at least as far as the facilities study stage under the existing rules by a tariff-prescribed 
deadline and can elect to complete the load interconnection process under the NYISO’s existing 
rules.  Projects in Transition Group B must have advanced at least as far as the completion of the 
system impact study by a tariff-prescribed deadline and can elect to enter the first Large Load 
Integration Study Process under the new Attachment LL rules, which transition process will not 
require the performance of a System Impact Study.  Finally, the NYISO proposes additional 
transition rules to facilitate the completion of certain ongoing system impact studies for 
information purposes as described in Part II.D.ii.  
The NYISO’s proposed transition framework—under which it seeks to balance parties’ 
expectations based on their relative progress against the proposal’s benefits and the need for 
administrable deadlines—is supported by ample precedent. Market participants do not have a 
reasonable expectation that market rules will remain unchanged.31 To the contrary, the 
Commission has stated that “there is always risk that tariffs and regulations can change, which is 
a risk that market participants take in a competitive market.”32 Consequently, where, as here, 
revisions in a Section 205 proposal are filed prospectively, such revisions do not implicate the 
filed rate doctrine or rule against retroactive ratemaking.33 Rather, the Commission balances any 
settled expectations against the benefits of the proposal, and has accepted the revisions where the 
benefits outweigh such expectations.34 As discussed in greater detail below, the NYISO’s 
proposal reasonably accounts for parties’ expectations by establishing transition rules based on 
each project’s relative stage of development, demonstrated commercial readiness, and size.35 
This is consistent with the Commission’s directive to reasonably consider existing commercial 
arrangements while drawing clear, administrable lines for the proposal’s effectiveness. 
c) 
Timeframe of Large Load Integration Procedures  
The NYISO proposes a timeframe for the performance of the Large Load Integration 
Study Process of between one year and six months and two years, including a 90-day period for 
the performance of the System Impact Study, as described in Part II.E.ii  The overall duration 
depends on when a Large Load Project satisfies the application requirements for entry into the

transmission system, identifying any Attachment Facilities and Network Upgrades required for 
the reliable interconnection of such project, including determining and allocating the cost 
estimates for such facilities, and determining the project’s Firm Withdrawal Service or Non-Firm 
Withdrawal Service amounts or, if requested, its eligibility to proceed as a Zero Withdrawal 
Service Load.   
d) 
Role of Transmission Owners 
The NYISO proposes to allocate the scope of responsibilities in the Large Load 
Integration Procedures between itself and the Transmission Owners as detailed in this filing 
letter.  The proposed allocation is similar to the allocation of responsibilities in the NYISO’s 
existing load interconnection procedures.  It accounts for the NYISO’s and Transmission 
Owners’ respective planning responsibilities, system knowledge, and access to underlying 
criteria and data.  The parallel division of work will also allow the NYISO and the Transmission 
Owners, working in parallel, to meet the proposed study timeframes and minimize inefficient 
and duplicative analyses. 
e) 
Assessment of Reliability Impacts and Determinations of 
Withdrawal Service 
The NYISO proposes that the interconnection of Large Loads must not adversely impact 
resource adequacy or transmission security.  To assess the impacts of Large Loads on the 
reliability of the New York State Transmission System, the NYISO proposes to establish a 
Resource Adequacy Impact Standard as described in Part II.G.ii and a Transmission Security 
Standard as described in Part II.G.iii.  The NYISO and Transmission Owners, as applicable, will 
apply these standards in evaluating the impacts of the proposed interconnection of Large Load 
Projects. 
The NYISO proposes to perform these evaluations for purposes of calculating a Large 
Load Project’s amount of Firm Withdrawal Service and Non-Firm Withdrawal Service and, if 
requested, its eligibility to be classified as a Zero Withdrawal Service Load.  In making this 
determination, the NYISO will account for available actions to mitigate any adverse reliability 
impacts as described in Part II.G.i.  In particular, a Large Load Project may mitigate its adverse 
impacts to resource adequacy by associating with new supply – an Associated Resource – or by 
taking sufficient Non-Firm Withdrawal Service.  Further, a Large Load Project may mitigate its 
adverse impacts on transmission security by agreeing to proceed with Network Upgrades that 
address the violation or by taking sufficient Non-Firm Withdrawal Service.  For certain 
transmission security violations that can only be resolved with Network Upgrades, the Large 
Load Project will be required to proceed with Network Upgrades.

c) 
The State Exempt Large Load Projects Proposal Is Consistent with 
Cooperative Federalism 
The NYPSC stated in the Show Cause Order proceeding that the FPA gives it the  
primary role in ensuring the adequacy of generation resources in New York, and that it intends to 
exercise its authority with respect to large load resource adequacy.203 Meanwhile, the 
Commission has jurisdiction over resource adequacy issues to the extent that they affect 
wholesale electricity market, interstate transmission, or bulk power system reliability matters.204  
The Commission’s interest in these types of resource adequacy issues is reflected in the Show 
Cause Order, including its informational report directive and its suggestion that the NYISO take 
other steps to address resource adequacy challenges.205  And the NYISO itself has resource 
adequacy responsibilities under applicable NERC, NPCC, and NYSRC requirements and its 
Commission-jurisdictional tariffs.   
 
Thus, resource adequacy implicates both federal and state jurisdiction.  Consistent with 
the Show Cause Order,206 the NYISO has designed the State Exempt Large Load Projects 
proposal to respect cooperative federalism.  As the Altman Affidavit explains,207 the NYISO 
needs to consider the resource adequacy implications of Firm Withdrawal Service awards in 
order to fulfill its reliability obligations.  The NYISO is not seeking to displace New York State’s 
resource adequacy authority or “targeting” state-jurisdictional activity.208  The NYISO is simply 
accounting for resource adequacy implications when deciding whether to make Commission-
jurisdictional transmission service available to Commission-jurisdictional Transmission 
Customers.  At the same time, the NYISO’s proposal would preserve state authority by enabling 
the NYDPS to determine that certain Large Loads should be allowed to receive firm service even 
if they would otherwise individually exceed the NYISO’s Resource Adequacy Impact Standard.  
Making this treatment unavailable to the extent that State Exempt Large Load Projects would 
collectively cause a resource adequacy violation is not an impermissible intrusion into state 
jurisdiction.  It is a reasonable safeguard to ensure that federal reliability requirements are 
maintained.

i. 
Overview of New Study Process 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission indicated that the NYISO’s tariff appears to 
lack sufficiently clear and consistent provisions establishing a study process for evaluating the 
provision of transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads that considers 
the unique characteristics and impacts of large loads on the transmission system, including 
identifying the Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades necessary to provide such 
service reliably and providing a non-binding good-faith estimate of the cost and the time to 
construct such facilities.228  The Commission further indicated that the NYISO’s tariff may not 
clearly and consistently require the NYISO or the Transmission Owners to conduct studies that 
evaluate the transmission system’s ability to withstand risks observed from analyzed large load 
behavior created by the large load at the point of interconnection, or any other necessary 
supplemental studies to evaluate the impact of providing transmission service to Eligible 
Customers on behalf of large loads.229 
The NYISO’s existing load interconnection procedures in Sections 3.9 and 4.5 of the 
OATT provide for it, in cooperation with the applicable Transmission Owner, to perform 
technical studies to determine whether the proposed interconnection may degrade system 
reliability or adversely affect the operation of the NYS Power System.230  The NYISO proposes 
to establish in place of these requirements a new Large Load Integration Study Process in 
Attachment LL of the OATT.  This process will include detailed, clear and consistent 
requirements for the evaluation of the impacts of the proposed interconnection of Large Load 
Projects in a manner that accounts for the unique operational characteristic of Large Loads, 
including identifying any Attachment Facilities or Network Upgrades required for the reliable 
interconnection of the Large Load and determining the type and amount of Withdrawal Service 
for the Large Load Project.   
In particular, the NYISO proposes an Initial Study Phase as described in this Part II.H in 
which the NYISO and Transmission Owners will perform certain initial analyses of the proposed 
interconnection and a System Impact Study.  These collectively will provide a Large Load 
Project with a preliminary assessment of the feasibility of its proposed interconnection and 
potential Attachment Facilities and Network Upgrades, including preliminary estimates of the 
costs and time to construct such facilities.  If an Eligible Customer elects to proceed with its 
Large Load Project, the NYISO will then perform an Assessment of Load Integration as 
described in Part II.I.i in parallel with the Transmission Owner’s performance of a Facilities 
Study as described in Part II.I.ii to identify both the required Attachment Facilities and Network 
Upgrades and to establish the final determination of Withdrawal Service that the project is 
eligible to obtain.

The NYISO proposes to perform the Large Load Integration Study Process on a clustered 
basis for a Group of Large Load Projects that have satisfied the application requirements 
described in Part II.F to enter the next available Group, rather than performing such study 
through serial, individual studies.231  As with the NYISO’s Cluster Study Process in its Standard 
Interconnection Procedures, which evaluates a cluster of Cluster Study Projects, it is just and 
reasonable for the NYISO to perform the Large Load Integration Study Process on a clustered 
basis.  As the Commission found in Order No. 2023 in adopting a cluster study process for 
generator interconnection requests, a group study increases efficiencies as the transmission 
provider can perform larger interconnection studies encompassing many proposed facilities, 
rather than individual studies for each customer.232  As described in the Nguyen Affidavit, a 
grouped study permits the NYISO and the Transmission Owners to evaluate the collective 
reliability effects of Large Load additions and to identify coordinated upgrades, rather than 
conducting overlapping serial studies that could produce duplicative or inconsistent solutions.233  
Although the addition of multiple projects and larger aggregate MW quantities increases the 
technical complexity of the study, the grouped approach provides a more comprehensive basis 
for assigning responsibility for shared impacts and allocating the costs of common Network 
Upgrades. 
The NYISO proposes that the study work in the Large Load Integration Study Process 
will be allocated between the NYISO and the Transmission Owners as detailed in this filing 
letter and as described in the Nguyen Affidavit.234  This approach reasonably allocates the study 
work to the entity with the relevant system knowledge, planning responsibility, and access to the 
underlying criteria and data.  The parallel division of work will also allow the NYISO and the 
Transmission Owners, working in parallel, to meet the proposed study timeframes and minimize 
inefficient and duplicative analyses.  The NYISO will perform the evaluation of the impacts of 
the proposed interconnections of Large Load Projects on the Bulk Electric System portion of the 
New York State Transmission System and identify any violations and adverse impacts on the 
Bulk Electric System caused by the project.  In particular, the NYISO will evaluate impacts on 
the Bulk Electric System to provide a consistent statewide assessment of bulk-system reliability 
and interregional effects.  If more than one project contributes to the violation, then the NYISO 
will provide the Transmission Owners with the projects’ respective contributions to the identified 
violations to facilitate the allocation of upgrade costs.

Explanation of the NYISO’s Proposal 
 
NYISO currently uses Constraint Specific Shortage Pricing (“CSSP”) to represent the 
price impact that transmission shortages have on LBMPs. The CSSP is supported by a six-step 
Transmission Demand Curve representing transmission shortage prices that increase in tandem 
with further utilization of a transmission facility’s Constraint Reliability Margin (“CRM”). The 
CRM is a portion of transmission facility transmission capacity that the NYISO has reserved 
between a predetermined market limit and the facility’s hard limit, i.e. its line rating, which 
serves to insulate the NYCA transmission system from severe overload risk by allowing 
transmission scarcity to be reflected in market prices. In times of severe transmission scarcity, 
i.e. when a transmission facility reaches 100% CRM utilization, flows across a transmission 
facility will near or meet the facility’s line rating and the facility’s Transmission Demand Curve 
will produce a transmission constraint price of $4,000/MWh.  
The NERC Transmission Loading Relief (“TLR”) process is used to filter/sort external 
transactions for curtailment, based on a transaction’s ability to affect flows across a given 
flowgate.  This process uses an individual transaction quantity-share de minimis threshold of 5% 
when determining whether the curtailment of an individual transaction will materially impact 
flows across a given flowgate. The NYISO applied similar materiality logic to the CSSP 
construct, specifically to the Transmission Demand Curve, in determining the $200/MWh bid 
price cap for NFWS Loads. 
The NYISO will use the 5% materiality threshold used in the NERC TLR process in 
determining which NFWS Loads have material impact on flows across a binding transmission 
constraint, i.e. an NFWS Load that has a minimum Shift Factor of 5% on a transmission 
constraint will be considered to have material impact on flows across that constraint. As 
discussed, when the Transmission Demand Curve binds at 100% CRM utilization, it produces a 
price of $4,000/MWh on the associated transmission constraint. NYISO believes this is the point 
at which it becomes most appropriate to ensure NFWS Loads that exacerbate this constraint are 
curtailed. An NFWS Load whose Shift Factor meets the 5% materiality threshold described 
above would, except in rare cases, receive a nodal price of $200/MWh when the correlated 
transmission constraint produces a $4,000/MWh price. By aligning the NFWS Load bid cap with 
this $200/MWh nodal LBMP, NYISO ensures that NFWS Loads that meet the 5% materiality 
threshold are curtailed automatically by the market optimization when the CRM of a relevant 
transmission facility is fully utilized, preventing the Large Load from exacerbating the constraint 
further and avoiding manual intervention by NYISO Grid Operators.  
The proposed bid cap ensures that Non-Firm Withdrawal Service Large Loads will be 
curtailed in advance of significant transmission security or resource adequacy shortage events.  It 
also increases the probability that Non-Firm Withdrawal Service Loads that most aggravate a 
given transmission constraint, i.e. those with higher Shift Factors on a given constraint, will be 
curtailed in advance of those that do not.  This results in a natural precipitation of NFWS Load 
curtailment priority that is grounded directly in reliability and automated by NYISO’s

The Curtailment Proposal Is Commission-Jurisdictional 
 
The NYISO is mindful that there questions may be raised regarding the jurisdictional 
status of its curtailment proposal. In particular, the Commission recently rejected substantial 
portions of PJM’s proposal to introduce an “Interim Resource Adequacy Service” (“IRAS”) and 
Bring Your Own New Capacity framework in its region.504  PJM defined IRAS as “a load 
reduction service through which New Large Loads reduce load as directed by the applicable 
Electric Distributor[.]”505 Among other determinations, the Commission found that PJM’s 
proposed tariff language appeared to be setting a retail rate because it would have established a 
“compensation rate for IRAS payable to the Eligible New Large Load.”506  Notably, the 
Commission stated that “a non-firm transmission service similar to Non-Firm Contract Demand 
transmission service, with appropriate adjustments, might be considered as a potential avenue to 
achieve some of the aims of PJM’s proposed IRAS framework.”507 
By contrast, the NYISO neither proposes to mandate any load reduction service of the 
kind presented IRAS  or otherwise, nor proposes any form of compensation for such a service. 
Rather, the NYISO is proposing to provide Transmission Customers taking service on behalf of 
Large Loads and Large Loads acting as their own LSEs with a new Commission-jurisdictional 
non-firm transmission service option with attributes similar to Non-Firm Contract Demand 
service, with appropriate adjustments,508 which aligns with the Commission’s guidance set forth 
in the IRAS Order. 
Unlike PJM under IRAS, the NYISO would not curtail NITS, or any other form of firm 
transmission service, to similarly situated firm loads.  Instead, the NYISO is proposing a new 
category of service to differently situated loads (i.e., loads voluntarily choosing to be served via  
Non-Firm Withdrawal Service instead of  Firm Withdrawal Service.)  The possibility of 
curtailment is a necessary component of Non-Firm Withdrawal Service because it ensures the 
reliability of the NYISO’s wholesale markets and transmission system during elevated demand 
conditions.509 A Large Load receiving Non-Firm Withdrawal Service will have been studied and 
found to have adverse impacts resource adequacy impacts that it has chosen not to mitigate.  The 
NYISO would not simply be relegating the Large Load to inferior service based on 
characteristics that touch on retail jurisdictional domains.  
Additionally, a CLLC is not entitled to compensation when it is curtailed under Non-Firm 
Withdrawal Service. Mandatory curtailment of Limited Withdrawal Service Loads when 
capacity exceeds the nodal $200/MWh price threshold is required to avoid adverse impacts to 
resource adequacy and/or transmission security. The NYISO’s proposed bid cap is a condition to

The NYISO is proposing to exclude Limited Withdrawal Service Loads, i.e., Loads that 
are not fully served via Firm Withdrawal Service, from participation in the ISO Administered 
Markets as a Demand Side Resource (e.g., Special Case Resource (“SCR”), Emergency Demand 
Response Program (“EDRP”), Distributed Energy Resource (“DER”) and Aggregations).515  It is 
reasonable to make Large Loads taking NFWS ineligible to receive compensation for demand 
reductions because Large Loads taking this service have voluntarily elected to take a lower level 
of transmission service in order to either avoid paying for Network Upgrades or to avoid 
bringing new ICAP supply to market to mitigate any resource adequacy and/or transmission 
security impacts they may cause, as determined in the LLIP.  Non-Firm Withdrawal Service 
Large Loads, by definition, are not entitled to consume Energy from the system at any time. 
Accordingly, NFWS Large Loads are not in a position to voluntarily reduce their consumption of 
Energy from the grid at all, let alone do so during the specific hours in which there would be a 
net benefit to the system and/or other customers by virtue of their voluntary demand reduction.516 
It follows that Large Loads taking NFWS are excluded from the Load forecasts that 
inform the Installed Reserve Margin (“IRM”) and Locational Minimum Installed Capacity 
Requirements (“LCRs”), do not create an ICAP obligation for their LSE and therefore Capacity 
Resources are not procured on their behalf through the ICAP auctions.  Large Loads with NFWS 
are not similarly situated to those with Firm Withdrawal Service. 
When a Large Load with Firm Withdrawal Service voluntarily registers to participate in 
the ISO Administered Markets as a Demand Side Resource, it is agreeing to forego its Firm 
Withdrawal Service Rights, i.e. agreeing to voluntarily curtail its Load, in exchange for payment 
when the requisite net benefit threshold is met. This payment is justified because the absence of a 
Large Load making its typical withdrawals from the system via its Firm Withdrawal Service 
during peak hours reduces NYISO’s net on-peak Capacity obligations and when the net benefits 
test is met and hence, the overall benefit of the reduced LBMP that results from dispatching such 
FWS Large Loads to reduce their consumption exceeds the cost of dispatching the more 
expensive generation resources.517  In other words, by qualifying as an ICAP Supplier and 
offering ICAP at auction, a Firm Withdrawal Service Load is reducing the net impact that its 
Load has on the outcomes of the ICAP market auctions, and reduces its LSE’s net ICAP 
obligations as a result.

Side Resource in the NYISO markets and thus receive compensation for voluntary demand

As previously stated, Large Loads taking some amount of Firm Withdrawal Service 
along with some amount of Non-Firm Withdrawal Service and/or that are partially Zero 
Withdrawal Service Loads, will be classified as Limited Withdrawal Service Load and must 
participate under the CLLC participation model. Like with other CLLCs, these “partial” Firm 
Withdrawal Service Large Loads will still be required to submit Energy Bids in the Day-Ahead 
Market whenever they seek to withdraw from the grid and will need to be dispatchable. It will be 
possible for Market Participants to “preserve” their Firm Withdrawal rights when participating 
under the CLLC participation model through the structuring of their bids, such that CLLC 
scheduling outcomes honor the Large Load’s right to in part consume Energy from the grid 
regardless of price.518     
e) 
Market Rules Applicable to Zero Withdrawal Service Loads 
(“ZWSL”)   
The NYISO is proposing to add new language to the Services Tariff to address the 
treatment of ZWSLs.  The introduction of a defined ZWSL voluntary option and related market 
rules is responsive to the Show Cause Order’s observation that the NYISO’s tariffs did “not 
appear to include a mechanism by which an Eligible Customer, on behalf of Eligible Load, 
would be charged for ancillary services commensurate with its usage of such services, 
particularly if such customer did not withdraw energy from the transmission system.”519  The 
ZWSL proposal is also compatible and practically implementable within the framework of the 
NYISO’s market design and financial reservation transmission model.    
The new ZWSL designation applies to a Large Load or portion thereof that is not 
permitted to physically withdraw Energy from the NYS Transmission System or has requested 
not to withdraw Energy from the NYS Transmission System and is served exclusively by a Co-
Located Resource(s) or Co-Located Local Generator.  The ZWSL designation is only relevant to 
co-located configurations, i.e., Large Load that cannot be served by front-of-the-meter 
generation or that a Market Participant has requested not be served by front-of-the-meter 
generation. ZWSL are not studied for and do not receive eligibility to receive any Withdrawal 
Services through the LLIP, i.e., do not have a right to withdraw from the grid to serve their Load.   
ZWSL status is similar to the BTM:NG Host Load concept under NYISO’s existing 
design, in that ZWSL is Load that exists behind-the-meter and is served exclusively by behind-

a configuration does not interface with the NYISO markets but, consistent with the general rule 
for ZWSL, would be subject to the Gross Load cost allocation methodology described in Part 
IV.B.ii.f and to the System Reliability Benefit Fee described in Part IV.B.ii.g. 
The ZWSL option may be attractive if it aligns with potential market participant’s 
business objectives or use cases, e.g., if the value of a faster development timeline makes it 
worthwhile for a Large Load to elect to take this option.520  For example, if a Co-Located 
Facility’s Point of Withdrawal is undersized relative to the amount of Load that is seeking to 
interconnect behind-the-meter, some or all of that Load may choose to classify as ZWSL and be 
served exclusively by behind-the-meter generation. 
ZWS Load is subject to the Gross Load cost allocation methodology described in Part 
IV.B.ii.f as it is, by definition, interconnected and synchronized to the NYS Transmission 
System and therefore benefits from the stability provided by Ancillary and Transmission 
Services. ZWS Load is additionally subject to the SRBF discussed in Part IV.B.ii.g. This is 
consistent with the Show Cause Order’s expressed concern that the NYISO’s Tariff does not 
appear to include a “mechanism by which an Eligible Customer [] would be charged for ancillary 
services commensurate with its usage of such services, particularly if such customer did not 
withdraw energy from the transmission system.”521 
As such, the NYISO’s proposal to provide a participation framework for Zero 
Withdrawal Service Loads appropriately accommodates the unique operating characteristics of 
this type of Large Load and is just and reasonable.

g) 
The System Reliability Benefit Fee 
The NYISO proposes to assess a System Reliability Benefit Fee (“SRBF”) under new 
OATT Section 6.24.  The SRBF would be “assessed to an LSE associated with the MW of (a) 
the portion of a Limited Withdrawal Service Load(s) that is not taking Firm Withdrawal Service 
and/or (b) a Co-Located Local Load(s) that is not included in the applicable LSE’s portion of 
Unforced Capacity Obligation the NYCA Minimum Unforced Capacity Requirement, in 
accordance with Section 5.11.1 of the Services Tariff.” 
The purpose of the SRBF is to allocate ICAP market costs Limited Withdrawal Service 
Loads, or portions thereof, not taking Firm Withdrawal Service in an amount roughly 
commensurate to the benefits they receive from ICAP Resources and the value of the reliability 
service that they provide during periods of low demand.  The SRBF will serve as a cost allocator 
for these Large Loads, which will benefit from reliable service despite not being required to pay 
ICAP market costs.    
As discussed in the Smith Affidavit,526 the SRBF will be assessed to the LSE taking 
service on behalf of a Limited Withdrawal Large Service Load.527  It is not a volumetric charge 
based on actual Large Load energy withdrawals, Instead, it will be based on the amount of Non-
Firm Withdrawal Service or Zero Withdrawal Service MW studied and authorized through the 
LLIP.  By tying the SRBF to authorized MW rather than actual MWh, the NYISO will charge 
these Large Loads for the reliability benefits they receive from the NYISO capacity market. 
Without the SRBF, these Large Loads would benefit from stable and reliable system operations 
without contributing correspondingly to the costs incurred to maintain those operations. The

Proposed Large Load Operating Requirements 
The NYISO proposes to revise Sections 3.5.2 and 13 of the Services Tariff to require 
Transmission Customers taking service on behalf of Large Loads to submit the following 
information to the NYISO: (i) six-second Real-Time telemetry; (ii) hourly revenue-grade meter

necessary operational visibility into and control over Large Loads, which will result in more 
accurate and reliable market solutions and operator decisions. Having clear operational 
requirements in place also protects customer interests by minimizing the need for costly out-of-
market actions to account for changes in Large Load behavior.

addition, the NYISO and/or CTO may request disconnection of a CLLC or a CLGC to avoid 
impermissible injections and/or withdrawals.  These actions are expected to be consistent with 
existing operating and communication procedures that exist today with transmission owners. 532 
This proposal is responsive to the Show Cause Order’s directive that the NYISO’s Tariff 
should include provisions addressing ongoing operational requirements for transmission 
customers taking transmission service on behalf of large load.533 The Commission specifically 
highlighted the absence of provisions requiring transmission customers to provide the NYISO

i. 
Overview and Eligibility

participation model in the Services Tariff for Co-Located Arrangements535—the Co-Located and 
Limited Load Configuration (“CLLC”) framework. 
 
ii. 
CLLC-Specific Definitions 
The NYISO proposes several definitions related to co-location. In particular, the NYISO 
proposes to define CLLC as: 
A configuration that consists of (a) a Co-Located Load that is a 
Limited Withdrawal Service Load participating with one or more 
Co-Located Resources, in accordance with Section 4.1.12 of the 
ISO Services Tariff, or (b) a stand-alone Limited Withdrawal 
Service Load. All components of the CLLC must be located 
behind a single Point of Interconnection. A Large Load taking only 
Firm Withdrawal Service may not participate in a CLLC. 
A Co-Located Resource(s) participating in a CLLC may not 
participate in the ISO Administered Markets through any other 
participation model. A Co-Located Resource that is a Hybrid 
Storage Resource cannot participate in a CLLC.  
The CLLC shall participate in the ISO-administered Energy and 
Ancillary Services markets as a single Resource that is capable of 
following the ISO’s dispatch instructions. In order to qualify for 
wholesale market participation, a CLLC must be able to inject or 
withdraw at least 1 MW of Energy to/from the transmission 
system. A CLLC will be required to submit Energy Bids consistent 
with the Withdrawal Service(s) being taken by the Co-Located 
Load and the manner in which the Market Participant seeks to 
exercise those Withdrawal Service rights within a given real-time 
market interval. The Co-Located Resource(s) in a CLLC shall 
participate in the ISO-administered Installed Capacity market as a 
single ICAP Supplier referred to as a Composite Co-Located 
Resource.536

An internal Bilateral Transaction provides a financial method for a NYCA Generator to

While PJM also administers co-optimized day-ahead and real-time energy and ancillary 
services markets and its transmission model involves Financial Transmission Rights somewhat 
akin to the NYISO’s TCCs, the NYISO’s transmission model is materially different from PJM’s 
because the NYISO’s financial reservation-based model does not involve any physical 
reservations for transmission service. 
Through the NYISO’s DAM and RTM software, internal New York generation resources 
compete, including with External Transactions, to be economically awarded an Energy schedule, 
which includes the necessary transmission service and ramp schedule. Additionally, the NYISO 
continuously redispatches the grid on a security-constrained, least-cost basis in order to 
maximize the efficient use of the system. As such, the total production cost to serve Load is 
minimized by the NYISO’s SCUC, RTC and RTD, which provides significant savings to Loads 
compared to a dispatch that matches Generator output to the demand of a specific sub-set of 
Loads.  
NYISO’s market constructs, specifically the Transmission Congestion Contract market, 
also provides a pathway to manage congestion cost (i.e., the Transmission Usage Charge 
associated with firm transmission) for instances where ex-ante price certainty is valuable. TCCs 
provide a voluntary financial hedge against Day-Ahead congestion costs without conferring a 
physical scheduling priority or altering the NYISO’s security-constrained dispatch. This 
separation permits customers to obtain greater cost certainty while preserving efficient, 
nondiscriminatory access to transmission capability for all market participants.  
The financial reservation model also accommodates materially different Large Load 
operating characteristics without creating administratively defined transmission priorities. A 
Large Load that can reduce withdrawals during constrained conditions may express that 
flexibility through its scheduling parameters and applicable operational requirements, while a 
Large Load that requires uninterrupted withdrawals (and whose interconnection supports such 
un-interrupted withdrawals) remains exposed to the costs associated with that service. The model 
therefore preserves a direct relationship between the service a customer values, the flexibility it 
provides, and the congestion costs it causes, rather than socializing those costs or embedding 
them in a new class of physical transmission rights. This supports efficient customer decisions 
regarding location, consumption, onsite supply, contractual hedging, and willingness to curtail. 
The model is also adaptable as system conditions and Large Load consumption change 
over time. Financial schedules and locational settlements can reflect the actual hourly—and, in 
real time, interval-specific—effects of a Large Load’s withdrawals, avoiding the need to 
establish a static physical reservation based on forecasts that may prove inaccurate or operating 
assumptions that may later change. That adaptability is especially valuable for Large Loads 
whose development timelines, utilization levels, and operating profiles may be uncertain. It 
reduces the risk that scarce transmission capability will be stranded or inefficiently reserved, 
protects other customers from subsidizing uneconomic uses of the system, and permits Large

The NYTOs will also propose four new two-party pro forma agreements that would be 
added to the NYISO OATT.  Specifically: (i) a Network Upgrade Cost Recovery Agreement; (ii) 
a Security Agreement; (iii) a Facilities Study Agreement; and (iv) a Large Load Interconnection 
Agreement.  The NYISO would not be a party to any of these arrangements.   
 
640 For the avoidance of doubt, the NYISO emphasizes that its arguments against implementing the PJM 
Co-Location Order Services in NYISO should not be interpreted as questioning the adoption of those services in 
PJM or other regions that choose to implement them.  The NYISO’s arguments here are only applicable to the 
NYISO region.     
641 Show Cause Order at P 41.

Hon. Debbie-Anne A. Reese  
 
 
November 16, 2026 
Page 125 
 
 
Similarly, the NYISO understands that the LS Power NY intends to make a Section 205 
filing to address its rate and cost recovery issues.  Because LS Power NY is an NTO without 
retail customers the NYISO understands that its filing will principally involve proposed revisions 
to NYISO OATT Schedule 10 (Rate Mechanism for the Recovery of the Regulated Transmission 
Facilities Charge) instead of OATT Section 5  
The NYISO is not a signatory to the NYTOs’ or NTOs’ FPA Section 205 filings.  It will 
play a ministerial role in electronically submitting their filings because they implicate NYISO 
tariffs as the NYISO has done for prior transmission owner rate filings made under their reserved 
rights.  The NYISO  reserves the right to comment on the NYTOs’ and NTOs’ proposals before 
the Commission.  In particular, the NYISO recognizes that the draft pro forma agreements will 
be important to resolving the cost-shifting questions raised by the Show Cause Order. And while 
the Show Cause Order envisioned the NYISO joining a three-party cost recovery agreement it 
did not foreclose reasonable alternatives.642 
 
VII. 
THE FPA SECTION 205 STANDARD OF REVIEW AND SEVERABILITY 
The Commission has explained that “[u]nder FPA section 205, the Commission is limited 
to considering the filing before it, . . . .”643  Federal courts have similarly noted that “[w]hen 
acting on a public utility’s rate filing under section 205, the Commission undertakes ‘an 
essentially passive and reactive role’ and restricts itself to evaluating the confined proposal.”644  
Courts have further acknowledged that “FERC has interpreted its authority to review rates under 
[the FPA] as limited to an inquiry into whether the rates proposed by a utility are reasonable—
and not to extend to determining whether a proposed rate schedule is more or less reasonable 
than alternative rate designs.”645 The Commission “is not required to choose the best solution, 
only a reasonable one.”646 
Adhering to these precedents and principles is especially appropriate in this proceeding.  
The NYISO’s proposal addresses a large number of operationally and legally complex questions 
in the context of the resource adequacy challenges facing New York.  This included considering 
jurisdictional issues, particularly the NYPSC’s views as a state regulator in the process of 
devising its own large load interconnection policies.  The NYISO’s proposal also had to be 
developed exceptionally quickly while balancing the interests of many parties in order to obtain 
super-majority stakeholder support. The proposal should therefore be judged on whether it 
produces just, reasonable, not unduly discriminatory, and lawful rules – not on whether it will 
result in the best imaginable solution in every instance.   
The Commission should also assess the NYISO’s proposals in light of the NYISO-
specific conditions and circumstances that shaped it.  As Chairman Swett noted in her 
concurrence to the Show Cause Order, the Commission “has long allowed different regional

FERC, 744 F.2d 871, 875-76 (D.C. Cir. 1984)).   
645 Cities of Bethany v. FERC, 727 F.2d 1131, 1136 (D.C. Cir. 1984).

transmission organizations to follow different rules, in recognition of regional variations . . . .”647  
The NYISO is starting from a different place, with different market, transmission, and 
interconnection rules that several other ISOs and RTOs.  It should not be a surprise, and is 
entirely reasonable, that NYISO would develop distinctive proposals to address the Show Cause 
Order’s concerns.  What matters is that the NYISO’s proposals are just, reasonable, and not 
unduly discriminatory on their own merits.  
Each element of this proposal is just and reasonable. Nevertheless, in the event the 
Commission deems it necessary, and to help facilitate the Commission’s acceptance of this filing 
without delay, NYISO provides notice that it consents to the Commission’s exercise of authority 
to modify and/or sever any element of the proposed OATT and Services Tariff language to the 
extent necessary and permitted under FPA section 205 and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. 
FERC,648 where such modification and/or severance is consistent with the NYISO’s overarching 
objectives in this filing. While the each of the reforms proposed in this filing is just and 
reasonable and act together to advance important objectives, they may also be considered 
separately. In particular, the NYISO consents to making any clarifications to its proposed tariff 
revisions that the Commission considers necessary to confirm that Firm and Non-Firm 
Withdrawal Services are Commission-jurisdictional transmission services.  
VIII. STAKEHOLDER APPROVAL 
The NYISO used the additional time provided by the Abeyance Order to conduct an 
expedited, extensive, and ultimately successful stakeholder process.  The NYISO held numerous 
stakeholder meetings and made presentations describing its evolving proposals on July 23, 
August 13, August 20, September 1, September 8, September 14, September 22, October 1, 
October 7, and October 14.  As the Smith Affidavit notes, this was not a straightforward effort 
but an iterative, intense, and thorough process.  The NYISO’s proposals are the product of 
countless hours of internal coordination amongst NYISO business units and stakeholder 
deliberations under significant time pressure.  The proposals have evolved and matured 
substantially since they were first proposed as a direct result of stakeholder feedback.  
A near-final version of the NYISO’s proposal was discussed at a joint meeting of the 
NYISO’s Business Issues Committee and Operating Committee on October 21.  Several 
changes, most notably the addition of the State Exempt Large Load Projects rules, were made in 
response to comments presented at joint meeting.  Subsequently, the NYISO’s final proposal was 
approved by the stakeholder Management Committee on October 28 by a 100% vote with 
abstentions.649  The proposal was then approved for filing by the NYISO’s independent Board of 
Directors on November 16.

FERC, 138 F.4th 531, 539 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (internal citations omitted).

subject to approval by the Management Committee, Business Issues Committee, and Operating Committee chairs.  
A number of such incremental changes have been incorporated into this filing.

Hon. Debbie-Anne A. Reese

The NYISO notes that the NYTOs’ and NTOs’ reserved filing rights are not subject to 
the NYISO’s shared governance procedures.  Their expected Section 205 filings therefore did 
not require stakeholder approval.  The NYTOs made an informational presentation describing 
their planned filing at the October 22 meeting of the NYISO’s stakeholder Transmission 
Planning Advisory Subcommittee.  
IX. 
REQUESTED EFFECTIVE DATES 
The NYISO respectfully requests a February 1, 2027 effective date for proposed OATT 
Attachment LL, i.e., the new LLIP, all new defined terms referenced in Attachment LL, Section 
3A of the OATT, all other OATT and Services Tariff revisions directly related to Attachment LL 
that are discussed in Parts II and III of this transmittal letter, and the BTM:NG sunsetting-related 
revisions referenced in Part IV.I above.  Because February 1 is less than 120 days after the date 
of this filing there is no need for a demonstration of good cause to support these proposed 
effective dates under Section 35.3 of the Commission’s regulations.  The NYISO expects to be 
ready to commence the optional pre-application process described proposed Attachment LL 
Section 44.5 on February 1.   
The requested February 1 effective date for the new Large Load Integration Procedures 
also means that the NYISO’s currently effective large load interconnection procedures in OATT 
Sections 3.9 and 4.5 will continue to be in effect for the entirety of the comment period.  This is 
more than eight months after the issuance of the Show Cause Order which will accommodate 
existing commercial arrangements. 
The NYISO is proposing to make its proposed tariff revisions related to its new market 
participation provisions for Large Loads, i.e., the revisions described in Part IV (other than Part 
IV.I) of this transmittal letter, effective on June 1, 2028.  There is good cause for allowing these 
provisions to become effective more than 120 days after this filing.  No Large Loads are 
expected to have completed the new LLIP, and thus to be able to utilize the new market 
participation provisions, until June 1, 2028 at the earliest.    
Finally, the NYISO’s is proposing to make its revision to Section 2 of the Services Tariff, 
which would effectuate the sunsetting of the existing BTM:NG program, effective on May 1, 
2029.  There is good cause for an effective date more than 120 days in the future because it will 
allow time for the handful of existing BTM:NG market participants to transition to alternative 
participation models.  
X. 
REQUEST TO CONTINUE ABEYANCE OF SHOW CAUSE PROCEEDINGS 
The Abeyance Order stated that, “[i]f  NYISO or Transmission Owners submit an FPA 
section 205 filing addressing the Commission’s preliminary findings in the Show Cause Order 
on or before November 16, 2026, then the obligation of the respondent(s) who have made such 
an FPA section 205 filing to file a response to the Show Cause Order will be suspended, and this 
proceeding will continue to be held in abeyance pending further Commission directive in this

Hon. Debbie-Anne A. Reese  
 
 
November 16, 2026 
Page 128 
 
 
proceeding.”650  The NYISO therefore requests that the Commission continue to hold the 
proceedings in Docket No. EL26-69-000, and the NYISO’s obligation to submit an answer to the 
Show Cause Order, in abeyance, pending Commission action on this filing. 
In addition, the NYISO requests that if the Commission were to require the NYISO to 
make additional tariff revisions before accepting the NYISO’s proposals under FPA Section 205 
that it hold the Show Cause proceedings in further abeyance for a reasonable time to give the 
NYISO an opportunity to prepare the necessary filing.    
XI. 
REQUEST FOR EXTENDED COMMENT PERIOD 
The NYISO respectfully requests that the Commission extend the standard 21-day 
comment period for FPA section 205 filings by one week.  The Commission has often granted 
extended comment periods for major filings that encompass numerous complex issues and tariff 
revisions that are likely to have substantial economic and reliability implications.  At the same 
time, the NYISO recognizes the importance of the issues addressed by this filing and 
understands the Commission’s desire to address large load issues rapidly.  The NYISO is 
mindful that the Commission has denied extension requests in certain recent involving large load 
matters.651  Accordingly, the NYISO submits that a brief one-week extension to the standard 
period so that comments would be due on December 14 instead of December 7 is reasonable 
given the number, complexity, and importance of the  proposals included in this filing.  Such an 
extension would also make a reasonable allowance for the comment period encompassing the 
Thanksgiving holiday. Because the earliest effective date requested in this filing is February 1, 
2027, i.e., two weeks beyond the default sixty-day period, a one-week extension would leave the 
Commission with slightly more time to review this filing than if the standard comment and 
notice periods applied.
